## 3. A long reply is sent back

Control: 8 non-empty lines, 2808 characters

Walled:  1 non-empty lines, 55 characters

```
TEXT   ## What `git rebase` does
       
       `git rebase` rewrites history by taking a sequence of commits and replaying them onto a new base commit, one at a time, rather than merging two histories together with a new merge commit. When you run `git rebase main` while on a feature branch, Git finds the common ancestor of your branch and `main`, temporarily sets aside every commit you've made since that ancestor, moves your branch pointer to the tip of `main`, and then reapplies each of your saved commits on top of that new tip in their original order. Each commit is essentially recreated as a new commit object with a new SHA (since its parent has changed), even though the diff it introduces is usually the same. This is the key conceptual difference from `git merge`: a merge preserves both histories exactly as they happened and stitches them together with a merge commit that has two parents, producing a non-linear graph, while a rebase produces a single straight line of commits as if you had started your work from the latest version of `main` all along. For example, suppose `main` has commits A → B → C, and you branched off at B to create commits D and E on `feature`. Running `git checkout feature && git rebase main` would replay D and E on top of C, producing A → B → C → D' → E' (note the primes — these are new commits with new hashes, not the original D and E). Your `feature` branch pointer now points to E', and it looks exactly as if you'd started coding from C in the first place.
       
       Rebasing is most commonly used to keep a feature branch up to date with `main` without cluttering history with merge commits, and to clean up your own commit history before sharing it — for instance with `git rebase -i HEAD~3` (interactive rebase), which lets you reorder, squash, edit, or drop the last three commits before pushing. A typical squash workflow: if you have three messy WIP commits ("fix typo", "wip", "actually fix bug"), an interactive rebase lets you mark the last two as `squash` (or `fixup`) so they collapse into the first, leaving one clean commit with a proper message. The major caveat, often summarized as "never rebase shared history," is that because rebasing creates new commit hashes, anyone else who has already pulled the original commits will have a diverging history from yours once you rebase and push — their local D/E and your new D'/E' are different objects with the same content but different parents, and reconciling that typically requires a force-push (`git push --force-with-lease`) on your end and a reset or re-pull on theirs. This is safe for local, not-yet-pushed commits or for branches only you work on, but risky for branches other collaborators are actively building on top of. A related but distinct use is `git rebase --onto`, which lets you replay a range of commits onto an arbitrary target rather than just the tip of another branch — useful when you need to move a subset of commits (say, commits from a branch that was itself branched off an already-merged feature) onto a different parent entirely, such as `git rebase --onto main old-feature-base my-branch`.
```
